title: Mahuri: breath within the ensemble
lead: A reed instrument beside drums, dancers and conch players: follow Mahuri through Odisha’s gatherings and the objects that preserve its story.

paragraphs: A small wooden instrument can lead us into a much larger gathering. In an Indian Council for Cultural Relations programme, the Muhuri has a double reed at one end and a flared wooden bell at the other. The same page places Mahuri beside dhol, nishan, tasha and jhanj in Bajasal, a dance associated there with western Odisha and marriage celebrations.

This is a useful place to begin listening: with one instrument inside a group. Follow the phrase it carries, then turn your attention to the drums and the dancers. What do you notice when you listen to their relationship? The question is an invitation for a welcomed performance, rather than a description of a recording we have heard.

blocks.title: A reed, a tube, a bell
paragraphs: The ICCR description gives us a starting shape. A museum object adds another. Berlin’s Ethnologisches Museum catalogues a Mahuri with a short wooden body, seven finger holes and a decorated metal bell. Its record identifies it as a double-reed instrument, while noting that the reed support and mouthpiece are missing from this particular example.

The wooden bell in the programme and the metal bell in the museum record should both remain in the story. They are descriptions of different examples; neither establishes one compulsory design for every Mahuri. When a musician is willing to explain their instrument, ask about its maker, materials and reed before assuming that a catalogue describes the object in their hands.

The museum’s English entry is marked as machine-translated. It supplies an inventory number, VII c 1005, and records a donation in 2019. That acquisition date does not date the instrument’s manufacture or the beginning of the tradition.

blocks.title: The company it keeps
paragraphs: In Kalahandi’s district account of Singh Baja, Mahuri appears alongside Nishan, Dhol, Tasa and Tal at marriage occasions. The account locates the form in places including Bhawanipatna, Lanjigarh and Koksara. It gives us a regional setting in which to understand an ensemble; it does not promise a performance on the day of a visit.

The ICCR programme describes the instrument’s sound as associated with auspicious occasions, including marriages, processions and temples. That is the programme’s cultural interpretation. The people hosting a particular occasion can explain what the music means there and how a visitor should take part.

Sambalpur’s district website uses the spelling Muhuri in its list of regional folk instruments. Mahuri and Muhuri both appear in the sources used here. Keeping those spellings visible helps a reader follow the records without treating one English spelling as a complete account of local naming.

blocks.title: Beside the conch in Ganjam
paragraphs: A different ensemble appears in the Eastern Zonal Cultural Centre’s account of Thakurani Jatra, printed in the 2012 Republic Day programme. It connects Jodi Sankha with Ganjam’s religious processions and describes conch playing coordinated with bodily movement. Dhol, Changu and Mahuri are named as accompanying instruments.

This connection brings us back to the Sankha story in this collection. Listening to the conch alone leaves part of the documented ensemble outside our attention. At an appropriate public occasion, notice who plays alongside whom, when movement changes, and how the group makes room for each sound.

blocks.title: A history to build with musicians
paragraphs: These sources give us an identifiable museum object and several accounts of performance settings. They do not establish the earliest Mahuri, a single place of invention or an uninterrupted lineage. A fuller history needs dated objects and documents alongside the knowledge of makers and players, with each account credited in its own terms.

A future conversation could begin with practical questions: Who taught you? Who makes or repairs your instrument? Which tunes belong to this occasion? Those answers would connect the object to the work of keeping music alive. They have not yet been collected for this article.

For now, carry one modest listening question with you: what changes when you follow the Mahuri through the ensemble? Ask permission before recording, and agree separately on any public sharing. The musician’s explanation deserves space beside the sound.

limits: A desk-researched introduction. Source spellings and object-specific materials are retained. Origins, maker histories and current performance availability remain unverified; no practitioner interview or independent human review is claimed.
